entries.clue: Threat to informer? (4,4,3,4)

blocks.note: The surface is selling you a day at the mall, but in British slang to grass somebody up is to 'shop' them, and that is the sense the first word carries.
Said to a snitch rather than a customer, the advertising line stops being an invitation and turns into a warning about how long the grassing will go on.

annotation.walkthrough: Vlad turns a shop-window slogan into menace by changing what one verb means. There is no wordplay to unpick here — the whole clue is the joke, and spotting it is the solve.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase works as a threat because 'shop' means to grass someone up, so the shopping slogan reads as a promise of informing until you collapse.

entries.clue: Youth is speaking about another: ‘Dickhead!’ (5,4)

indicators.note: A story written about a subject goes all the way round it, and that is what the outer word does to the letters dropped between its ends.

blocks.note: somebody who is speaking says
another of what the clue has just called a youth is a lad
the first letter of Dick — its head

annotation.walkthrough: The rudeness is a red herring: only the head of the name Dick is wanted. And 'another' leans on the definition, because another youth is simply a lad.
annotation.definitionFit: Salad days are the green, inexperienced years Cleopatra looks back on in Shakespeare, so the phrase is an idiom for being young rather than a plain synonym.

entries.clue: B-list occasionally spoken about is going round (7)

indicators.note: Something done occasionally happens every so often rather than every time, so only every other letter is picked up.
To be about a thing is to be all round it, so the longer piece closes over the shorter one.

blocks.note: an oral exam is a spoken one
every other letter of B-LIST: B, I and T

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is showbiz chatter and both instructions pass as ordinary description. Watch 'spoken': here it is a straight synonym, not an invitation to listen.
annotation.definitionFit: Anything orbital travels a circular path around something else — the motorway that rings London is called the orbital for exactly that reason.

entries.clue: Singer Tom with suite trashed (8)

indicators.note: To trash a hotel room is to leave nothing where it was, and letters treated that way come back in a different order.

blocks.note: three of the eight letters, taken as they stand
the other five letters of the fodder

annotation.walkthrough: A rock star and a wrecked hotel suite make a perfectly good sentence, which is the point — neither word is doing the job it appears to be doing.
annotation.definitionFit: A titmouse is a small songbird, the tit of British gardens, so 'Singer' points at it by what the bird does rather than naming the family.

entries.clue: I get emotional about returning to London’s original theatre (5)

indicators.note: To write about something is to go round it, so the single letter ends up enclosed by the word that follows.
Whatever returns comes back the way it went, so those letters are read in the opposite order.

blocks.note: the opening letter of London
to get emotional is to cry
the pronoun taken at face value as a letter

annotation.walkthrough: The Lyric on Shaftesbury Avenue is a real playhouse, so the last word is the definition even though it looks like part of the scene it describes.
annotation.definitionFit: Lyric is the name of a London playhouse, so 'theatre' defines the answer by example — the class the name belongs to, not a synonym for it.

entries.clue: Long for a drink? (4,2,3)

blocks.note: a yard is a long measure, three feet of it
the two prepositions swap freely when a vessel is named by what it holds
ale is the drink being measured out

annotation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: read straight it is a thirsty sigh, read as instructions it builds the thing itself. A clue that is all definition and all wordplay is called an &lit.
annotation.definitionFit: A yard of ale is the yard-long glass, and the beer in it, that pubs keep for challenges — so the clue describes it exactly: something long, for drinking.

entries.clue: Turn left, perhaps, after park entrance – positive? (6)

indicators.note: The way into a word is its first letter, so this one asks for the opening of the word beside it and nothing else.

blocks.note: the turn that doubles back on itself is a U-turn
the entrance to PARK is its opening letter
left is one example of a side, which 'perhaps' flags

annotation.walkthrough: The comma after the first word is doing real work: that word stands alone rather than joining the driving instruction the rest of the surface promises.
annotation.definitionFit: The upside of a situation is its positive aspect, so both are nouns naming the good half of something rather than the adjective they look like.

entries.clue: Complaining in bar (7)

blocks.note: to rail at something is to complain loudly about it
a piece of ironmongery: the bar-work guarding a staircase or a balcony

annotation.walkthrough: Three words, no wordplay and two meanings of one word: a verb of protest and a piece of ironmongery. The little 'in' is all that joins them.
annotation.definitionFit: To rail at somebody is to complain bitterly, and a railing is the bar-work of a fence — one word, a verb sense and a noun sense.

entries.clue: Forces serviceman, might you say? (5)

blocks.note: Read straight this is any enlisted member of the armed services, which is the picture the surface wants: a soldier, a sailor, an airman.
The question mark admits the pun. The man meant is the one who takes the service — the chaplain attached to a regiment, and no fighting man at all.

annotation.walkthrough: Everything turns on the word 'service': the Forces have one meaning for it and the chapel quite another, and the answer is the man who belongs to both.
annotation.definitionFit: British soldiers borrowed the Spanish and Italian word for father to name their chaplain, so this is Forces slang for him rather than an official rank.

entries.clue: Throw back nameless catch at sea (7)

indicators.note: Something nameless has had its name taken off it, and the abbreviation for name is the single letter N.

blocks.note: to lob a ball is to throw it
the stern is the back end of a boat

annotation.walkthrough: 'Throw back' reads as one action and is two separate jobs, which is the whole difficulty. N for name is worth learning: setters delete it constantly.
annotation.definitionFit: A lobster is literally a catch — what comes up in the pots — so the definition names the answer by the trade that lands it.

entries.clue: Withdraw having committed a further offence as reported (7)

indicators.note: Anything reported is passed on by mouth, so what matters is how the phrase sounds and not how it is written down.

blocks.note: to sin again is to re-sin, so somebody who has offended a second time has RE-SINNED

annotation.walkthrough: The joke is that a second offence and a cancellation sound identical. RE- for 'again' is worth filing away, since setters lean on it constantly.
annotation.definitionFit: To rescind a rule is to cancel it officially, which is what 'withdraw' means when a body takes back something it has already issued.

entries.clue: Newton going, ‘You shouldn’t point!’ (3)

indicators.note: Something going is on its way out, so the letter named beside it leaves the word it was sitting in.

blocks.note: don't is what you say for you shouldn't
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

annotation.walkthrough: Vlad hides a physicist inside a telling-off, and the exclamation mark helps by making the last word look like rudeness rather than punctuation.
annotation.definitionFit: A dot is a point in the typographical sense — the full stop, the decimal marker — rather than the sharp end of anything.

entries.clue: Previously keeping flashy eroticist very happy (2,5,4)

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it, and a word that keeps another closes right around it.

blocks.note: once means previously, as in once upon a time
a loud tie is a flashy one
Anaïs Nin, the diarist who wrote erotica

annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as gossip about somebody's taste in books, and nothing in it hints at delight. Anaïs Nin is standing crossword currency: file the three letters away.
annotation.definitionFit: Being on cloud nine is the idiom for elation, a whole phrase meaning delighted where none of its three words says anything of the kind alone.

entries.clue: Mainly competent rating (4,6)

blocks.note: able means competent
the main is the open sea, so the man described as 'mainly' is a man of the sea

annotation.walkthrough: The main is an old word for the open sea, and 'mainly' is pointing at that rather than at 'for the most part'. The surface passes as faint praise.
annotation.definitionFit: In the navy a rating is any sailor below officer rank, and the answer is one of those ranks — so the definition names the class it sits in.

entries.clue: Hit wicket – AUS 1 down (spinner finally bowled over) (9)

indicators.note: Whatever has been hit does not stay in the shape it was in, so these letters land in a new order.
In cricket a batter who is down is out, and the numeral named beside it goes out of the fodder too.
Taken finally means taken at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word in front joins in.

blocks.note: WICKET hands over its letters once the 1 has gone
1 is the Roman numeral I, and one down is one out, so that I leaves WICKET
the scoreboard's Australia, taken as three letters
the last letter of spinneR

annotation.walkthrough: A whole cricket scoreboard, and every word of it is working. The definition hides best of all, because being knocked over sounds like still more cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: To be bowled over is to be knocked flat by amazement, the same figurative sense as being struck with awe — both name astonishment, not impact.

entries.clue: Knocked back the drink (over a gallon) for some considerable time (4)

definitions.note: The answer is plural in form but names one unbroken stretch, which is why a singular phrase defines it: nobody waits for one age.

indicators.note: Knocking a drink back is swallowing it, but knocking anything back sends it the other way, so the letters run in reverse.
What is over something lies across it and covers it, so the shorter piece ends up tucked inside.

blocks.note: the drink is the sea, as in falling into it
G is the abbreviation for gallon

annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs in a pub and not one of them stays there: the drink is salt water, and knocking it back is an instruction rather than a swallow.
annotation.definitionFit: Ages is the everyday exaggeration for a long stretch — 'I waited ages' — so it matches the loose, unmeasured quantity the definition describes.

entries.clue: Synonyms to begin with: fly, go off, make a run for it (9)

indicators.note: The phrase asks for the start of the word in front of it, so its opening letter is all that survives.

blocks.note: the opening letter of Synonyms
a ked is the wingless fly that lives on sheep
eggs that go off addle

annotation.walkthrough: 'Synonyms' is lovely misdirection: it promises a list of words meaning the same thing, and only its first letter is wanted. The ked is worth meeting.
annotation.definitionFit: To skedaddle is to clear off in a hurry, which is just what making a run for it describes — the American slang verb for a hasty exit.

entries.clue: Call service engineers initially for correction (8)

indicators.note: What happens initially happens first, so the corps named beside it takes the front of the word rather than following on.

blocks.note: the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, known to the army as REME
to call somebody is to dial them

annotation.walkthrough: REME turns up whenever a clue mentions service engineers, and is worth knowing alongside RE for the Royal Engineers. The surface is a helpdesk; the answer is a classroom.
annotation.definitionFit: Remedial work is work done to put something right — remedial classes, remedial repairs — so the answer is the adjective for anything meant as a correction.

entries.clue: Coming back discontented, negotiates very low price, a bargain (4)

indicators.note: Something coming back retraces its route, so those letters are read from the far end to the near one.
A word robbed of its contents keeps only its outermost letters, which is what leaves it hollow.

blocks.note: NEGOTIATES emptied of everything between its ends leaves N and S
1p is about as low as a price gets: the Roman numeral I and p for penny

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a haggler at work, and the price in it is literal — one penny, written as a figure and a letter. Nothing is negotiated but the spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: A snip is British slang for a bargain, something going far below what it is worth, so the noun sense is wanted and not the cut of scissors.

entries.clue: Less sensible son gets involved making little difference (7)

indicators.note: Somebody who gets involved is drawn into the middle of the business, and the letter goes the same way.

blocks.note: the more inane a thing is, the less difference it makes
S is the abbreviation for son

annotation.walkthrough: Comparatives are what make this work: definition and wordplay are both '-er' forms, which is easy to miss while the surface is busy being about a family.
annotation.definitionFit: Insaner is the comparative of insane, so 'less sensible' matches it grade for grade — one step further from sound judgement rather than the full condition.

entries.clue: US comedian put away for drugs in decline (10)

indicators.note: Swapping one thing for another puts the first where the second was, so these three letters take over the place of those two.

blocks.note: Ellen DeGeneres, the American comic and chat-show host
Es are ecstasy tablets, and those are the two letters standing at the end of the name
to put away a big meal is to eat it, and that is what moves in

annotation.walkthrough: The name is spelt out in full and then loses its tail. E for ecstasy is standard crossword drug slang, and here the setter wants two of them at once.
annotation.definitionFit: To degenerate is to decline — to fall away from a better state — so verb and definition are plain synonyms in their intransitive sense.

entries.clue: Current Republican leading on the surface is a moron (7)

indicators.note: Whatever lies on the surface covers what is underneath, so one word closes over the two letters and hides them.

blocks.note: the runner who is leading is ahead
I is the physicist's symbol for electric current
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

annotation.walkthrough: Politics is the misdirection: the opening two words are not a person at all but two single letters, one out of physics and one off a ballot paper.
annotation.definitionFit: An airhead is somebody with nothing much between the ears, so 'a moron' matches it insult for insult in ordinary speech.

entries.clue: A green revolution of sorts (6)

indicators.note: A revolution turns everything over, and letters caught up in one do not come back in the order they went in.

blocks.note: the six letters of the fodder

annotation.walkthrough: 'A green revolution' is a real phrase about farming, which is exactly why it does not look like six letters waiting to be rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: Genera are the groups biology sorts living things into, one rank above species, so 'sorts' is the plural noun in its classifying sense.

entries.clue: Loudly complain after sailors originally aboard leave port? (7,4)

indicators.note: Doing something loudly means doing it audibly, so that word is to be heard rather than read.
What a word was originally is what it starts as, so only its opening letter is used.
To be aboard is to be on the ship, inside it, so the letter goes within the word beside it.

blocks.note: to desert a post is to leave it
the opening letter of sailors
to complain is to whine, and whine said aloud is spelt this way instead

annotation.walkthrough: 'Leave port' reads as one nautical phrase and the clue splits it in two, taking the first word for wordplay and the second for the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Port is one particular fortified dessert wine, so the definition works by example: it names a member of the class the answer names.

entries.clue: Make editor ultimately responsible for such columns (5)

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective naming a style of column, so the plural noun phrase points at the order the style belongs to rather than substituting word for word.

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the end, so the final letter of the word beside it is the one taken.

blocks.note: do and make share the sense of performing a task
the last letter of editoR
i/c is short for in charge, which is what being responsible for something is

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is an office row about who carries the blame. Learn i/c for 'in charge': two letters that hide easily inside an innocent phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Doric names the oldest and plainest of the Greek architectural orders, so 'such columns' points at a style of building rather than at any one pillar.

entries.clue: Vlad’s past being ideal (5)

blocks.note: the setter of this puzzle is Vlad, so Vlad's is I'm
something past happened ago

annotation.walkthrough: Setters sign their own clues: whenever a Guardian puzzle names its setter, read it as 'I'. It is the same convention as 'the setter' meaning ME.
annotation.definitionFit: In psychoanalysis an imago is the idealised picture of a parent carried into adult life, so 'ideal' is that technical noun rather than the everyday adjective.

entries.clue: Take main road around valley (3)

indicators.note: Turning a thing around leaves it facing the other way, so those two letters are read in the opposite order.

blocks.note: R is the prescription sign for take, from the Latin recipe
the A1 is the main road north, and its 1 is written as the letter I

annotation.walkthrough: Numbers standing in for letters is a Vlad habit: the 1 of the A1 is an I, exactly as the 1 in 14 down is. R for 'take' comes off a doctor's pad.
annotation.definitionFit: A ria is a river valley drowned by the sea, so 'valley' names the landform the answer is a flooded example of.

entries.clue: Neither partner recalled mentioning bread lines (7)

indicators.note: To recall something is to call it back, and letters called back arrive in the reverse order.
Mentioning a thing is saying it, so what follows is to be heard rather than spelt.

blocks.note: neither always travels with nor, so that is its partner
bread is dough, and the sound of dough is spelt out here in the French manner

annotation.walkthrough: Bread and dough are slang for money either way round, but here it is only the sound that matters. 'Lines' is the crossword's usual way of saying verse.
annotation.definitionFit: A rondeau is a short French poem turning on repeated lines, so 'lines' is the standing crossword shorthand for a piece of verse.

entries.clue: Flavouring from America is in demand (7)

indicators.note: The smallest word in the clue is the instruction: one piece goes inside another, exactly as being in demand puts you within it.

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for America
a demand is a need
the word itself, taken as two letters

annotation.walkthrough: 'In demand' is a phrase the surface needs and the wordplay pulls apart. The most ordinary word in the clue is the one carrying the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Aniseed is the seed of the anise plant, used to flavour drinks and sweets, so 'Flavouring' names it by the job it does in a kitchen.

entries.clue: What Telford had a lot of to attract Romeo – sex (6,9)

indicators.note: To attract a thing is to draw it in towards you, which is where that single letter finishes up.

blocks.clueFragment: What Telford had a lot of
blocks.note: Thomas Telford built the canals, so canal knowledge is what he had in quantity
R is Romeo in the radio alphabet

annotation.walkthrough: Thomas Telford was the great canal engineer, and the joke is that fourteen letters of specialist expertise need only one more to turn into something quite different.
annotation.definitionFit: Carnal knowledge is the legal and biblical idiom for sexual intercourse, so the whole phrase means 'sex' where neither of its words does alone.
